newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia fray over Timor not expected to hit investment.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia fray over Timor not expected to hit investment.

text.p: The ugly break-up of an East Timor conference by a government-backed youth mob has given Malaysia a black eye but it is an aberration that won't affect investment, political and economic analysts said on Tuesday.

Police detained 66 local activists and journalists and deported another 46 foreigners after the youth group smashed its way into the conference, overturning furniture, ripping down banners and hectoring the activists with loudspeakers.

It was a shocking scene in a country that puts great value on courtesy and non-confrontation. But analysts said that because it was so dissonant with Malaysia's political culture, the incident would not damage its image in the long term.

"It is bound to affect Malaysia's image for a short while," said University Sains Malaysia professor Chandra Muzaffar, who heads a human rights group called JUST. "It is something which Malaysians are not proud of.
"But it is not the kind of thing that will make people think twice about investing in Malaysia," Chandra said.
A foreign research director at a stock brokerage agreed.

"I don't see it having much relevance to the stock market," said the director who did not want to be named. "The relevant questions are: Is the country stable? Yes. Is the economy okay? Yes. Is the political situation likely to deteriorate? No."
Political analyst Rustan Sani said Malaysia had never relied on its reputation as a robust democracy to attract investments in the first place.
"I don't think foreign investors are very concerned about the defence of democracy, as long as you do not go around arresting people like this every day."
It was the biggest crackdown on dissent since October 1987 when police arrested 106 people, including top politicians and activists, under the Internal Security Act.
"You don't often see that sort of violence in Malaysia," said Bruce Gale, the Singapore-based regional manager of the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy.
"I'd be inclined to see it as an abberation. It might be of concern if this is how future matters are settled. But for now, I'd be inclined to give Malaysia the benefit of the doubt."
He said what was worrying about the incident was that top government leaders, including Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, have so far declined to condemn the mob action.

Indonesia's invasion and annexation of the former Portuguese colony of East Timor is a taboo subject with its neighbours. The Kuala Lumpur conference was to be held just ahead of Tuesday's fifth anniversary of the 1991 killings of 50 demonstrators in the East Timor capital of Dili by Indonesian troops.

"I think it will be assumed by Indonesia and in other Asian capitals that the Malaysian government was behind (the disruption of the conference)," Gale said. "And Jakarta will appreciate the effort by the Malaysians."
Gale said the incident would probably not have an impact on Malaysia's newly-launched "multi-media super corridor", a zone that aims to attract world-class information technology firms.
"When people look at it more closely, they'll see it isn't related to major cleavages in Malaysian society," he said.
